question: What is the meaning of the use of standard ontologies in relation to certifications, standards, classifications and compliance, legal and regulatory information?
data_group: certifications, standards, classifications and compliance, legal and regulatory information
description: The use of standard ontologies in relation to certifications, standards, classifications, and compliance, legal, and regulatory information is crucial for ensuring interoperability and consistency across different domains. This approach supports the FAIR principle (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable) and facilitates controlled access, modification, and authentication of information. Additionally, it helps in harmonizing technical implementation with internationally recognized standards and existing ontologies, thus avoiding duplication of efforts and maximizing the intended benefits of sustainable production and consumption practices.

Sustainable Production and Consumption 48 (2024) 248–268

Studies show that ontologies can address the functional requirements 
that are stated by the EC for DPPs by providing a structured and standard 
method for data representation and exchange (Gligoric et al., 2019; 
Kedir et al., 2021; Sauter et al., 2019). The principles of Linked Data are 
in alignment with the open, standard, and interoperable format needed 
for DPPs and offer flexible and reliable solution that meets the re­
quirements outlined by the EC for the successful implementation of 
DPPs. Further, the use of these technologies supports the notion of the 
“need-to-know” principle, as they can be used to implement secure ac­
cess control and data privacy measures (Kirrane et al., 2017), addressing 
one of the challenges related to data privacy and confidentially issues 
faced while developing DPPs (Ducuing and Reich, 2023; Gharib et al., 
2020; G¨otz et al., 2022). Ontologies can define relationships and roles, 
facilitating controlled access, and modification of information (Brewster 
et al., 2020; Li et al., 2018). With the concept of provenance in the se­
mantic web, the author of information can be authenticated, and the 
reliability of the information can be ensured (Samuel and K¨onig-Ries, 
2022). Additionally, these technologies are based on global standards 
and operate under open licenses, aligning with FAIR principle (findable, 
accessible, interoperable and reusable) (Bizer et al., 2008). 
In this study, we use an ontology-based approach to develop modular 
ontologies for DPP. Additionally, it is important to harmonize the 
technical implementation of DPPs with internationally recognized 
standards and existing ontologies in order to avoid duplication of efforts 
and maximize the intended benefits that can be achieved by DPPs (G¨otz 
et al., 2022). In line with this, and in anticipation of forthcoming stan­
dards like ISO/DIS 59004, which is currently under development, stra­
tegies are being considered to enrich data with additional information 
and description. In doing so, we have utilized some of the vocabularies 
defined in the portions of the standard currently available to the public, 
despite these being only a small fraction of the complete standard. This 
effort aims to make the data globally understandable. Moreover, existing 
ontologies, including building topology ontology (BOT) (Rasmussen 
et al., 2020), building product ontology (BPO) (Wagner et al., 2022), 
material properties ontology (MAT) (Poveda-Villal´on and Ch´avez-Feria, 
2020), brick schema ontology (BRICK) (Balaji et al., 2016), RealEsta­
teCore ontology (REC) (Hammar et al., 2019) and the environment 
ontology (ENVO) (Buttigieg et al., 2016) are used to semantically 
represent and enrich data. Given the complexity of capturing the diverse 
content of DPPs in a single ontology, and with the aim of promoting the 
consistency and universality of the DPP, ontology design patterns are 
utilized to create well-structured and semantically rich ontologies 
tailored to the context of our DPP. These patterns enable the reuse of 
standard ontologies – that is, a set of terms and relationships commonly 
used across various domains – thus ensuring interoperability between 
different ontologies (Blomqvist et al., 2023; Shimizu et al., 2023). 
2.3. Modular ontology and ontology design patterns 
DPP covers information related to all aspects of a product, starting 
from its origin to end-of-life management. It records the history of a 
product during its use stage. This information can grow to be compre­
hensive. Modeling such big data using an ontology-based approach re­
sults in a sizable and monolithic ontology. This outcome presents a 
recurring challenge in ontology development as it contradicts the 
fundamental principle that ontologies should be reusable (Hitzler, 
2021).
